title: Elicit and use evidence of student thinking
subtitle: Continuously gather what students actually understand — and let that evidence change what you do next, in the moment and in the next lesson.

sections.sources: Source: NCTM, Principles to Actions (2014) · Wiliam, formative assessment · Adding It Up (2001).

blocks.text: Effective teaching uses evidence of student thinking to assess progress toward mathematical understanding and to adjust instruction continually in ways that support and extend learning.

This is formative assessment in the truest sense: not a grade, but **information the teacher acts on**. Eliciting means making thinking visible — through questions, written work, and talk. Using it means the evidence actually changes the next move: which idea to highlight, when to reteach, when to press on. Evidence you collect but don’t respond to isn’t this practice; it’s just paperwork.
What it looks like in grades 6–8

items: The teacher circulating and reading student work *as it happens*, adjusting on the fly.
Tasks and exit tickets designed to reveal reasoning, not just a right/wrong answer.
Next lesson visibly shaped by what yesterday’s evidence showed.
Common misconceptions surfaced on purpose and used as teaching material.

yes.title: We want to see & hear
items: The teacher monitoring and responding in real time
Exit tickets that ask “how do you know?”
Instruction that changes based on evidence
Student errors mined for what they reveal

no.title: We should *not* see
items: “Thumbs up if you got it” as the only check
The same lesson tomorrow regardless of today’s results
Only final answers looked at, never the reasoning

blocks.text: Where it lives in our toolbelt

This practice runs through [Check-for-Understanding & Exit Tickets](/math/approach/cfu-exit-tickets) and the monitoring inside [Fluency Practice](/math/approach/fluency-practice). It is the “monitor” and “select” work of the [5 Practices](/math/approach/five-practices), and it’s why [Error Analysis](/math/approach/error-analysis) treats mistakes as evidence worth teaching from.
By shaping instruction to what students actually need, this practice serves *all five* strands — it’s the feedback loop that keeps the rest honest.
Pick one exit-ticket prompt that asks for reasoning, read the stack tonight, and let it decide your first five minutes tomorrow. Evidence used to change one move is worth more than a binder of data.
